title: What Getting Better Would Look Like
objective: Choose one art-form skill to develop, and write the measure that will show it changed.

blocks.text: BUILD · Art · Week 1. Trinity Arts Award Bronze. What Getting Better Would Look Like.
Objective: choose one art-form skill to develop, and write the measure that will show it changed.
Success evidence: one chosen skill, a checkable goal, the proof page and today's date on your card.

Your skill comes off your own artwork and off the skill cards in the approved pack. You talk about marks, tools and numbers. You are not asked about your home, your family, your beliefs or how you look. Nobody in this room is asked about theirs.
Identity here means what your own work keeps choosing. Today you choose one skill to build on.
40 minutes. Offline.

This deck evidences Bronze Part A, Explore the arts as a participant. Part A requires active participation in any art form, improvement, and a summary of what they learnt; this deck sets the measure that improvement will later be shown against. Bronze attempted rule, quoted from the register: "ONE Attempted allowed overall. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass." The evidence file cap for the whole Bronze level is 10 files, so plan what is kept. The three assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, and communication.

Delivery is through a validated centre; confirm local validation and an adviser trained at Bronze before assessment. Neither is asserted as completed here. Core, Extend and Challenge are support routes inside Bronze, not different awards. The prompts and sample quantities are teaching scaffolds, not extra assessment requirements. Scribe only the pupil’s own words. Store evidence by part; one cumulative file per part is a suggested four-file plan within the ten-file cap.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Baseline sheets out on desks before pupils sit down, word side up. A pupil hunting for last lesson's sheet will not read the word on it.
stages.data-ta2: If a pupil says their whole art is bad, ask them to read their one word out loud. Work from that word only, and do not add a second.

blocks.text: A skill is one action you can practise
Last lesson you made one piece.
You wrote three words for what it does well.
You wrote one word for what it does not.
That one word is where today starts.
Today you pick one skill to build.
A skill is one action you can practise.
Shading is a skill. Art is too broad for this small goal.
Name one action in your chosen art form.
Too big means nobody can tell if it changed.
Read the skill-is-one-thing line once and leave it on the board. Without it pupils write down a whole art form and there is nothing to measure in six weeks.
You need three things: your baseline sheet, one skill card and a pencil.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Show both plans yourself, on the board. Do not read a pupil's card out as the weak one.

blocks.text: Two plans, six weeks apart
Here are two plans from two makers.
Maker one wrote: I will get better at art.
Six weeks on, nobody could tell.
There was nothing to hold up and check.
Maker two wrote: I will shade five steps with no gaps.
Six weeks on they held up the strip.
The gaps had gone, so the change showed.
Both makers worked just as hard.
One plan could be checked. One could not.

items: 1 · pick one skill, not a whole art form.
2 · make the skill small enough to see.
3 · set a measure you can count.
4 · write it down and date it.

blocks.text: A measure is the proof you will look for later.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Model on your own baseline sheet, not on a pupil's. Write the card in front of them so the card is seen being made.

blocks.text: I choose my skill and my measure
My baseline word was flat.
Flat means my work has no dark and no light.
So my skill is shading. I write that word on the card.
Shading is one thing my hand does.
Now I make it smaller still.
I pick shading with a pencil, in one small box.
A small skill is easy to test.

blocks.caption: Four steps, and the last one names your evidence
blocks.title: From baseline word to measure
blocks.alt: Boxes labelled READ, NAME, MEASURE, PROOF. Four steps, and the last one names your evidence

blocks.text: Next comes the measure, and this part is hard.
A measure has a number in it, or a can-do.
I write: I can shade five steps from light to dark.
Five is the number, so five can be counted.
Then I add where the proof will live.
My proof is one tone strip on page four of my arts log.
I name the page, not the whole folder.
In the arts log is not a place. Page four is.
Last I write today's date on the card.
Write the card where the group can see all four lines at once: skill, measure, proof, date. The four lines are the thing being taught, not the shading.
Watch the order. Skill first, then measure, then proof.
A measure needs a count or a feature someone can check.

stages.title: We Do · label and explain
stages.data-ta1: Use the model activity, then transfer the idea to the learner’s own work. Allow speech, pointing or a scribe.

data.heading: Label the checks you can see
data.instruction: Look at A, B and C. Label each sample with a check it shows. Point to the part that lets you check it.

categories.label: I can make three tones that differ
I can draw four gaps of the same width
I can keep my marks inside the edge

items.label: Label A
items.feedback: The three patches go from light to dark. The tones can be checked side by side.

items.label: Label B
items.feedback: Five lines make four gaps. Compare the gaps to check their width.

items.label: Label C
items.feedback: The filled part stays inside the outline. This check uses a clear feature, not a score.

data.discussion: Which check could help with your skill? You may choose a count or a feature. Say how someone could check it.
data.staffNote: These are examples, not compulsory goals. Accept any clear, checkable measure suited to the learner’s art form. The annotation is practice; their own skill card records their own choice.

stages.data-ta2: These are examples, not compulsory goals. Accept any clear, checkable measure suited to the learner’s art form. The annotation is practice; their own skill card records their own choice.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Both measures up at once. Let the group find the one that can be held against something.

blocks.text: A measure somebody else can check
Now look at two measures for the same skill.
The skill is mixing colour.
The first one says: get better at mixing.
Ask who checks that, and there is no answer.
The second says: mix one green that matches the swatch.
Anyone can hold the mix next to the swatch.

boxes.head: CAN BE CHECKED
boxes.line1: mix one green to match the swatch
boxes.line2: hold the mix next to it and look

boxes.head: CANNOT BE CHECKED
boxes.line2: there is nothing to hold it against

blocks.caption: Same skill, and only one measure can be proved
blocks.title: Checkable against not checkable
blocks.alt: Boxes labelled CAN BE CHECKED, CANNOT BE CHECKED. Same skill, and only one measure can be proved

blocks.text: So your measure needs two things.
It needs a number, or a can-do.
It needs a thing to hold it against.
That thing can be a swatch, a strip or a ruled line.
It can also be your own week one piece.
Old work is the fairest thing to check against.
You are not racing anybody else in this room.
One more rule: one skill only.
If two skills appear, choose one to focus on first.

items: 1 · name the skill in three words or less.
2 · name a count or a visible feature to check.
3 · name what you will hold it against.
4 · name the page the proof will live on.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Keep the earlier model visible for this paired check. Pupils have not made their independent work yet; do not ask for a sheet that does not exist.

blocks.text: Test the model’s measure
Use the model skill card shown earlier. Your own piece comes next.
Work in twos with the model skill card.
Read the model’s measure out loud.
Then ask the check question: how would I know?
If they can tell you how, put a tick by it.
A tick means the measure can be proved.
If they cannot, write the word how by it.
How means the measure needs a clear check.
Help them name a count or a feature to look for.
Do not change their skill. The skill is theirs.
Then swap roles, with two minutes each way.
You are not judging the art. You are testing the words.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Scribe the exact words. Do not upgrade a pupil's measure into a harder one, and do not swap their skill for a neater one.
stages.data-ta2: If a pupil ties the skill to home, family, their body or how they look, say: today the card names a mark and a number. Then point at the skill line and move on. Do not comment.

blocks.text: Your skill, your measure, your proof
Work on your own now.
Use a pencil, so a measure can be made smaller.
Write your skill on the top line of the card.
Use three words or less.
Write your measure: a count or a feature to check.
Start the measure with the words I can.
Then write what you will hold it against.
Then write the page the proof will live on.
The proof is a page in your arts log.
Name the page, not the whole folder.
Last, write today's date on the card.

items: Core · Choose one skill and a measure from the cards. Say how to test it and name the proof file and page.
Extend · name one skill, write a checkable measure, and name the proof page.
Challenge · as Extend, and write the first small step you will take next lesson.

blocks.text: If you finish early, write the date you will check the measure.
Add a date so the stages of your work are easy to follow.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: The named adult reads the measure back word for word, then writes it in the class record. Acknowledge the choice, and keep the pupil’s words unchanged.

blocks.text: Say it once to an adult
Read your measure to the adult at your table.
They read it back to you word for word.
Then they ask the check question: how would I know?
You answer with the proof and the page.
If the check is unclear, name what they should look for.
That adult is your audience today.
They write your measure in the class record, next to your name.
Now pick one thing that happens next. Keep the measure, make it smaller, or add one step.
Write your pick on the card, under the date.
Your card goes in the arts log folder, not in your bag.
Add this work to your Part A file. Write the file name and page number. For a sound or video clip, give the file name and the time where your evidence starts.

print.intro: Write the skill card in pencil, and keep every line on the card itself rather than on this sheet. You may speak, point or write; keep your own words in the record.
focusRows: One skill named in three words or less, taken from the baseline word
One checkable measure, starting with the words I can
The thing it will be held against, and the arts log page the proof will live on
tiers: Choose one skill and a measure from the cards. Say how to test it and name the proof file and page.
Name one skill, write a checkable measure, and name the proof page.
As Extend, and write the first small step you will take next lesson.
checks: One specific arts skill is named, with a clear action to practise.
The measure names a count or a feature that someone else can check.
The card names what the work will be held against, such as a swatch, a strip or the week one piece.
The arts log page is named, and today's date is written on the card.
The evidence locator gives the actual file name plus page, slide or timecode.
